symptoms: Yellowing and withering of the central heart leaf, which dries while outer leaves remain green.
Drooping and breaking of leaf petioles at the pseudostem junction.
Yellowish bacterial ooze (slime) exuding from a freshly cut pseudostem cross-section.
Progressive wilting and collapse of the whole mat from the centre outward.
Grey-brown discolouration of vascular bundles visible in longitudinal section.
Sudden, complete wilting of branches on one side of the tree while leaves remain attached.
Dark brown to black staining of the wood beneath the bark on affected stems.
Dull green then yellow-brown leaf discolouration followed by leaf curl and dieback.
Premature ripening (green or over-ripe cherries dropping) on wilting branches.
Brown vascular discolouration visible in a cross-section of the affected stem.
Dark brown to black soot-like spots across the leaf surface.
Premature drying of heavily spotted leaves.
Yellowing then browning from leaf tips and margins inward.
No bacterial ooze on cut tissue.
Whitish winding tunnels inside leaves.
Papery window-like patches; early leaf drop.
Black charcoal-like powdery coating on leaves.
Often follows scale insects and mealybugs.
Small circular orange to brown powdery pustules on both leaf surfaces.
Powdery residue rubs off on fingers.
Long, narrow white to yellow streaks parallel to the veins.
Severe stunting and small cobs in young plants.

containment: Uproot and destroy infected mats immediately, including all adjacent symptomatic plants.
Deep-bury infected debris in a pit at least 1 metre deep, away from the farm, and leave the pit open to direct sunlight.
Isolate infected fields: restrict movement of soil, suckers, and tools from affected to healthy plots.
sanitation: Flame-sterilize Macha harvesting knives over an open fire before and after every cut.
Wash tools with a 10% household bleach solution between plants when flaming is not possible.
Wash hands and boots after handling infected plants before entering healthy plots.
chemical_biological: No effective chemical curative treatment exists for Xanthomonas vasicola pv. musacearum.
Follow clean cultural practice guidelines: there is no registered bactericide that cures an infected mat.
prevention: Plant disease-free suckers from certified or visibly healthy mother plants only.
Do not replant Enset in the same hole for 6-12 months; keep the soil exposed to sunlight.
Space mats widely so harvesting tools never touch neighbouring plants.
Use tolerant landraces such as Lemat, Beshute, and Yiregiye where available.
Inspect mats weekly during the rainy season (June-September) and remove symptomatic plants early.

containment: Uproot and burn infected coffee trees completely, including the root system.
Deep-bury or burn all infected debris; do not compost affected material.
Quarantine the affected plot and prevent movement of uprooted stumps or soil to healthy fields.
sanitation: Disinfect all harvesting and pruning tools with a 10% bleach solution or by flaming between trees.
Disinfect boots and wash hands after working in infected plots.
Do not share seedlings or tools between infected and non-infected farms.
chemical_biological: No effective chemical curative treatment is available for Fusarium xylarioides.
Soil drenching with registered fungicides is not reliable; follow clean cultural practice guidelines instead.
Consider biological soil amendments (e.g., Trichoderma-enriched compost) as a preventive measure in replanted plots.
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seedlings of tolerant varieties where available.
Do not replant coffee in the same hole where an infected tree was removed for at least 12 months.
Practice crop rotation or fallow with non-host cover crops before replanting.
Maintain tree vigour with mulching and proper shade management to reduce stress-related susceptibility.
Monitor plantations monthly and uproot any tree showing early one-sided wilting.
